rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companion says he did not force the man into transgression: he was already far from truth, and the companion only enticed him to respond.
rows.anchor: هو تجاوز الحد في العصيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's enticement affects those already unstable in judgment, inclined to sin, and far from the right path; he invites without compulsion.
rows.anchor: فإن إغواى الشيطان إنما يوثر فيمن كان مختل الرأي مائلا إلى الفجور ضالا عن طريق الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This limited role of Satan matches his admission that he had no authority over people beyond inviting them, which they chose to follow.
rows.anchor: وما كان لي عليكم من سلطان إلا أن دعوتكم فاستجبتم لي

rows.speaker: الحديث
rows.claim: A hadith says the messenger has no power to guide; if guidance were his, everyone would believe, while Iblis only adorns and does not control misguidance.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث إنما أنا رسول وليس إلى من الهداية شيء ولو كانت الهداية إلي لآمن كل من في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narration turns to God's reply by posing the question of what God will say to Adam and his worldly companion.
rows.anchor: كأنه قيل فماذا قال الله لابن آدم وشيطانه المقيض له في الدنيا فقيل قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God addresses them at the scene of reckoning and requital, where disputing offers no benefit.
rows.anchor: أي في موقف الحساب والجزاء إذ لا فائدة في ذلك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say this rebuke addresses disbelievers; the dispute in God's presence in 39:31 concerns believers contesting wrongs, while 38:64 describes the dispute in Hell.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم : هذا الخطاب في الكفار وأما قوله ثم إنكم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God had warned them through revealed books and messengers during earthly moral responsibility, leaving no excuse for following Satan and rejecting truth.
rows.anchor: على الطغيان في دار الكسب والتكليف في كتبي وألسنة رسلي فما تركت لكم حجة علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning clause is circumstantial and explains the prohibition; its time is the present of the dispute, while the warning was already delivered in worldly life. The bāʾ may be extra or mark transitive usage of qaddama as taqaddama.
rows.anchor: والجملة حال فيها تعليل للنهي على معنى لا تختصموا وقد صح عندكم وعلمتم أني قدمت إليكم بالوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's decree of promise and threat cannot be changed; forgiving some sinners is specification of a general threat, and there is no such specification for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: لا يغير قولي في الوعد والوعيد فما يظهر في الوقت هو الذي قضيته في الأزل لا مبدل له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evidence for pardon particularizes the threat rather than changing it; in the case of unbelievers the threat remains general and unqualified.
rows.anchor: فإن دلائل العفو تدل على تخصيص الوعيد يعني ولا مخصص في حق الكفار فالوعيد على عمومه في حقهم

rows.speaker: الجلال الدواني
rows.claim: Al-Dawwani reports that some scholars allow God to forgo a threatened punishment, but not a promised reward; a hadith and Arab usage treat this as generosity, unlike breaking a good promise.
rows.anchor: قال الجلال الدواني في شرح العضد ذهب بعض العلماء إلى أن الخلف في الوعيد جائز على الله تعالى لا في الوعد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says the sky will rotate like a millstone and sway with its inhabitants like a ship at sea.
rows.anchor: قيل تدور السماء كما تدور الرحى وتتكفأ بأهلها تكفأ السفينة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account has the sky's parts convulse and its angelic inhabitants surge and mingle from fear.
rows.anchor: وقيل يختلج أجزاؤها بعضها في بعض ويموج أهلها بعضهم في بعض ويختلطون وهم الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains leave the earth and become fine dust.
rows.anchor: أي تزول عن وجه الأرض فتصير هباء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the mountains travel like clouds, then split apart in transit and end like fluffed wool.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم تسير الجبال كما تسير السحاب ثم تنشق أثناء السير حتى تصير آخره كالعهن المنفوش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains' disappearance resembles a wayfarer annihilated when the majesty of divine disclosure appears, leaving no trace.
rows.anchor: ومثله وجود السالك عند تجلي الجلال بالفناء فإنه لا يبقى منه أثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal nouns mūran and sayran emphasize that the sky's motion and the mountains' travel are extraordinary and beyond familiar limits.
rows.anchor: وتأكيد الفعلين بمصدريهما للإيذان بغرابتهما وخروجهما عن الحدود المعهودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ is explanatory; the sentence answers an omitted condition: once this happens, there is woe for them on that day.
rows.anchor: الفاء فصيحة والجملة جواب شرط محذوف أي إذا وقع ذلك المور والسيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe woe is specifically for those who deny God, His messenger, and the Day of Judgment; it does not exclude punishment of sinful believers.
rows.anchor: وهو لا ينافي تعذيب غير المكذبين من أهل الكبائر لأن الويل الذي هو العذاب الشديد إنما هو للمكذبين بالله ورسوله وبيوم الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase depicts an intense plunge into false claims, including mocking the Quran, denying the Prophet, and rejecting resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي اندفاع عجيب في الأباطيل والأكاذيب وبالفارسي در شروع كردن بأقوال باطلة كه استهزا بقرء آنست

rows.speaker: فتح الرحمن
rows.claim: Fath al-Rahman explains khawḍ as stumbling in falsehood, likened to wading and plunging into water.
rows.anchor: قال في فتح الرحمن : الخوض التخبط في الأباطيل شبه بخوض الماء وغوصه

rows.speaker: حواشي الكشاف
rows.claim: The Kashshaf marginalia says khawḍ can cover any subject but became conventional for falsehood, just as iḥḍār became conventional for being brought to punishment.
rows.anchor: وفي حواشي الكشاف الخوض من المعاني الغالية فإنه يصلح في الخوض في كل شيء إلا أنه غلب في الخوض في الأباطيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is a reproachful epithet, not a limiting description that distinguishes one subset of deniers from others.
rows.anchor: وقوله الذين هم في خوض ليس صفة قصد بها تخصيص المكذبين وتمييزهم وإنما هو للذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They amuse themselves and remain occupied in disbelief.
rows.anchor: يلهون ويتشاغلون بكفرهم

words: يَوْمَ يُدَعُّونَ إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daʿʿ is forceful pushing; the expression evokes pushing a stumbling person and then driving the condemned violently toward Hell.
rows.anchor: الدع الدفع الشديد وأصله أن يقال للعاثر دع دع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are driven with hands bound to their necks and forelocks pulled to their feet, pushed into the Fire on their faces or backs.
rows.anchor: بأن تغل أيديهم إلى أعناقهم وتجمع نواصيهم إلى أقدامهم فيدفعون إلى النار دفعا على وجوههم وفي أقفيتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm may be an apposition to the day the sky heaves, or a time adjunct for an understood statement introducing the next verse.
rows.anchor: ويوم إما بدل من يوم تمور أو ظرف لقول مقدر قبل قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement is an address spoken by the keepers of the Fire.
rows.anchor: أي يقال لهم من قبل خزنة النار هذه النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bihā attaches to tukadhdhibūn: they denied the revelation that spoke of this Fire.
rows.anchor: متعلق بقوله : {تكذبون} أي تكذبون الوحي الناطق بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question rebukes them for calling the Quranic warning sorcery: is the now-visible Fire sorcery too? Fronting the predicate focuses the reproach.
rows.anchor: توبيخ وتقريع لهم حيث كانوا يسمونه سحرا وتقديم الخبر لأنه محط الإنكار ومدار توبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The star may be considered generically; hawā can describe its setting, while a related usage describes rising or ascending.
rows.anchor: غربه وطلوعه يقال هوى يهوى من الثاني هويا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath governs idhā, used here as a general time detached from its future force; an oath is a present speech act, so it can swear now by a later setting.
rows.anchor: والعامل في إذا القسم أي أقسم فإنه بمعنى مطلق الوقت منسلخ عن معنى الاستقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God swears by the star when it sets because stars guide travelers on land and ships at sea along the right course.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الله تعالى أقسم بالنجم حين هوى أي وقت هويه لأن شأنه أن يهتدي به الساري إلى مسالك الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath's answer is that Muhammad never left the path of truth, the road of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: هو جواب القسم أي ما عدل عن طريق الحق الذي هو مسلك الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This denies the kind of error alleged by the phrase 'He found you astray' in 93:7: before and after revelation the Prophet worshipped God, affirmed unity, and avoided reprehensible conduct.
rows.anchor: وهذا دليل على أن قوله ووجدك ضالا ليس من ضلال الغي فإنه عليه السلام قبل الوحي وبعده لم يزل يعبد ربه ويوحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast with Adam, of whom scripture says he disobeyed and went astray, highlights the Prophet's virtue: God says Muhammad did not stray or err.
rows.anchor: وفيه بيان فضل النبي عليه السلام حيث أن الله تعالى قال في حق آدم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines ghayy as ignorance grounded in a false belief, unlike a complete absence of belief; it is narrower than ḍalāl, which includes errors of speech, action, character, and belief.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب الغي جهل من اعتقاد فاسد وذلك أن الجهل قد يكون من كون الإنسان غير معتقد أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayy is specified after the broader term ḍalāl to emphasize sound belief; the Prophet never held a false belief and possessed complete guidance.
rows.anchor: فعطفه على ما ضل من عطف الخاص على العام للاهتمام بشأن الاعتقاد بمعنى أنه فرق بين الغي والضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh accused Muhammad of leaving his ancestors' religion and speaking on his own; this sūra answers them, and 'your companion' reminds them they knew his blameless life and excellent guidance.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يقولون ضل محمد عن دين آبائه وخرج عن الطريق وتقول شيئا من تلقاء نفسه فرد الله عليهم بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites Rumi as presenting the Quran as guarded from error, neither astrology, geomancy, nor dreams, but divine revelation.
rows.anchor: نى نجومست ونى رملست ونه خواب

rows.speaker: صوفيان
rows.claim: The Sufis call it heart-revelation: the heart is God's place of regard and, when aware, is guarded against error.
rows.anchor: وحى دل كويند اورا صوفيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited saying that a believer sees by God's light supports the image of a heart protected from error and forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: مؤمنا ينظر بنور الله شدى از خطا وسهو ايمن آمدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If waḥy means scripture, Gabriel taught by bringing it down, reciting, and explaining it; if it means inspiration, he taught by conveying it to the Prophet's heart, as in 26:193–194.
rows.anchor: هذا على أن يكون الوحي بمعنى الكتاب وإن كان بمعنى الإلهام فتعليمه بتبليغه إلى قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective is annexed to its agent, like ḥasan al-wajh; an omitted noun is understood, meaning an angel mighty in strength, Gabriel.
rows.anchor: من إضافة الصفة إلى فاعلها مثل حسن الوجه والموصوف محذوف أي ملك شديد قواه وهو جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel's strength is illustrated by carrying Lot's towns from subterranean waters on a wing, bringing down Thamud with a cry, and blowing Iblis from the Holy Land to a distant Indian mountain.
rows.anchor: أنه قلع قرى قوم لوط من الماء الأسود الذي تحت الثرى وحملها على جناحه ورفعها إلى السماء

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib connects mirra with a tightly twisted cord; the dictionaries give it meanings including bodily strength, sound judgment, firmness, and a strong rope, and dhū mirra denotes Gabriel.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب : أمررت الحبل إذا فتلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-istawā explains how Gabriel taught: he stood firm in his created form, not the human forms he adopted when delivering revelation.
rows.anchor: عطف على علمه بطريق التفسير فإنه إلى قوله ما أوحى بيان لكيفية التعليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel's original form had six hundred jeweled wings; at other times he appeared as Dihya, a guest to Abraham, or an adversary to David.
rows.anchor: واستقر على صورته التي خلقه الله عليها وله ستمائة جناح موشحا أي مزينا بالجواهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Hira, Gabriel appeared from the east, filled the horizon, and overwhelmed the Prophet, who fell as Moses had at Sinai; Gabriel then took human form, embraced him, and brushed dust from his face.
rows.anchor: فطلع له جبريل من المشرق فسد الأرض من المغرب وملأ الأفق فخر رسول الله كما خر موسى في جبل الطور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A worldly body cannot bear a vision beyond its rational capacity; the author says no prophet but Muhammad saw Gabriel in his created form, twice, on earth and during the ascent at the Sidrah.
rows.anchor: فإن الجسد وهو في الدنيا لا يتحمل رؤية ما هو خارج عن طور العقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The horizon's rising and setting also image the human being: spirit is elevated and body low, as the spirit rises from the world of spirits and sets in embodied existence.
rows.anchor: مثل روح الإنسان وجسده فإن الروح علوي والجسد سفلي وقد طلع من عالم الأرواح وغرب في عالم الأجساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel intended to draw near to the Prophet at Hira; dunuww can mean closeness in essence or by relation, and applies to time, place, or rank.
rows.anchor: أي أراد الدنو من النبي عليه السلام حال كونه في جبل حراء والدنو القرب بالذات أو بالحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tadallā means to hang down while remaining attached: Gabriel extended from the highest horizon and approached the Prophet.
rows.anchor: التدلي استرسال مع تعلق أي استرسل من الأفق الأعلى مع تعلقه به فدنا من النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author illustrates the root with hanging fruit and dangling legs; a report about lowering a rope to the lowest earth means reaching God's knowledge, power, and dominion everywhere.
rows.anchor: لو دليتم بحبل إلى الأرض السفلى لهبط على الله أي على علمه وقدرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāba qawsayn measures the distance between them by two Arab bows; Arabs measured spans by a bow, matching the Quran's Arabic idiom.
rows.anchor: من قسى العرب أي مقدارهما في القرب وذكر القوس لأن القرآن نزل بلغة العرب والعرب تجعل مساحة الأشياء بالقوس

rows.speaker: معالم التنزيل
rows.claim: Maʿālim al-Tanzīl explains the measure as the space between a bow and its string, with qaws standing for the bowstring.
rows.anchor: معالم التنزيل معنى قوله كان بين جبرائيل ومحمد عليهما السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation recalls Arab allies joining their bows to seal friendship and a mutual defense pact.
rows.anchor: وأصله أن الحليفين من العرب كانا إذا أرادا عقد الصفاء والعهد خرجا بقوسيهما فألصقا بينهما

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the distance as two cubits, a cubit being called a bow because it is used to measure length.
rows.anchor: وقيل قدر ذراعين ويسمى الذراع قوسا لأنه يقاس به المذروع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distance was near without being contact, yet close enough for transmission: it is the familiar respectful distance of intimate companions conversing.
rows.anchor: فلم يكن قريبا قرب التصاق ولا بعيدا بحيث لا يتأتى معه الإفادة والاستفادة وهو الحد المعهود في مجالسة الأحباء المتأدبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative is from the hearers' perspective, not divine uncertainty: human observers might judge the distance two bows or closer, as with 'or more' in 37:147.
rows.anchor: فأو للشك من جهة العباد كما أن كلمة لعل كذلك في مواضع من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From 'then he drew near' through 'or nearer' the distance represents intimate connection and confirms that the Prophet heard the revelation without misleading separation.
rows.anchor: والمراد أي من قوله ثم دنا إلى قوله أو أدنى تمثيل ملكة الاتصال وتحقيق استماعه لما أوحى إليه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the approach literally: as Gabriel neared the Prophet he diminished, then appeared in his usual form at two bows' distance so the Prophet recognized him.
rows.anchor: وحمله بعضهم على حقيقته حيث قال فكلما دنا جبريل من النبي عليهما السلام انتقص فلما قرب منه مقدار قوسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel conveyed to God's servant, meaning the Prophet; 'servant' is an honorific relation, as in the opening of the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: أي جبرائيل {إلى عبده} أي عبد الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implicit 'of God' is omitted before the explicit servant because it is obvious, like the implicit earth in the phrase 'on its back' in 35:45.
rows.anchor: وإضماره قبل الذكر لغاية ظهوره كما في قوله تعالى ما ترك على ظهرها من دابة

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reads the dispute as veiled people arguing over created forms without witnessing the Real's unity amid their perception of multiplicity.
rows.anchor: وفي التأويلات النجمية يشير إلى مماراة المحتجبين عن الحق بالخلق ومجادلتهم في شهود الخلق من دون الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in raʾāhu refers to Gabriel; the Prophet saw him in his true form once more during one of the descents on the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: الضمير البارز في رآه لجبريل ونزلة منصوب نصب الظرف الذي هو مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazlatan is an adverbial accusative meaning one more time, since the noun denotes a single occurrence of an action.
rows.anchor: لأن الفعلة اسم للمرة من الفعل فكانت في حكمها والمعنى وبالله لقد رأى محمد جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet made repeated ascents to seek a reduction in the prescribed prayers; Gabriel remained behind at the Sidrah, saying that an inch farther would burn him, and the Prophet saw him there with six hundred wings shedding pearls and rubies.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنه كان للنبي عليه السلام في ليلة المعراج عرجات لمسألة التخفيف من إعداد الصلوات المفروضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sidrat al-Muntahā is a lote tree in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne; its fruit resembles large jars, its leaves elephant ears, rivers spring from its root, and its shade extends seventy years' travel.
rows.anchor: وهي شجرة نبق في السماء السابعة عن يمين العرش ثمرها كقلال هجر وورقها كآذان الفيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿInda may attach to raʾā or be a circumstantial phrase describing Gabriel, a created being seen at a particular place.
rows.anchor: وعند يجوز أن يكون متعلقا برأى وأن يكون حالا من المفعول المراد به جبرائيل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes al-muntahā as a verbal noun meaning ending, or as a place noun for the terminal point, as if it stood at the end of Paradise.
rows.anchor: والمنتهى مصدر ميمي بمعنى الانتهاء كما قال الزمخشري أو اسم مكان بمعنى موضع الانتهاء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says angels end there and cannot pass it; Gabriel's station is exclusive, just as the community may share Eden without reaching the Prophet's special station.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ينتهي إليها الملائكة ولا يتجاوزونها لأن جبرائيل رسول الملائكة إذا لم يتجاوزها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says creaturely knowledge and deeds terminate there: ordinary good deeds reach it through angels, while the most sincere deeds of the elect pass beyond angelic conveyance into the spiritual realm, known only to God.
rows.anchor: وقيل إليها ينتهي علم الخلائق وأعمالهم ولا يعلم أحدا ما وراءها وذلك لأن الأعمال الصالحة في عليين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations place the endpoint of martyrs' souls there, or say rulings descend from above while effects ascend from below.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ينتهي إليها أرواح الشهداء لأنها في أرض الجنان أو ينتهي إليها ما يهبط من فوقها من الأحكام

rows.speaker: الكاشفي
rows.claim: Al-Kashifi says angels flew around the tree, in a comparison to golden forms or beings.
rows.anchor: كما قال الكاشفي : وكويند بر حوالى آن فرشتكان طيران ميكردند ون روانهاى زرين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says divine lights veiled the tree when God manifested to it, as He manifested to the mountain; unlike the mountain, it endured because it belonged to the stronger realm of the unseen.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يغشاها سبحان أنوار الله حين تجلى لها كما تجلى للجبل لكنها كانت أقوى من الجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tree's strength is contrasted with the mountain's: the mountain belongs to the weak physical realm, while the Sidrah belongs to the powerful malakūt.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن الجبل كان في عالم الملك الضعيف والسدرة في عالم الملكوت القوى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view has immense flocks of angels covering the tree like ravens on a tree, worshipping there or visiting it for blessing as people visit the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يغشاها الجم الغفير من الملائكة أمثال الغربان حين يقعن على الشجر يعبدون الله تعالى عندها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further account says angels descended to greet the Prophet, each bringing a heavenly tray of gifts to scatter before him.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يغشاها الملائكة النازلون للقاء النبي عليه السلام فإنهم استأذنوا للقائه فأذن لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says the Prophet received three gifts at the Sidrah: the five prayers, the closing verses of al-Baqara, and forgiveness for followers who die without associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: إنه أعطى رسول الله عندها يعني السدرة ثلاثا

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reads the Sidrah as the tree of divine oneness: its innumerable branches and blossoms are manifestations of names and attributes, while its trunk is concealed beneath them; oneness is identical with unity in reality but distinct by rational consideration.
rows.anchor: وفي التأويلات النجمية يشير إلى تعظيم المظاهر الأسمائية والصفاتية الجمالية اللطفية والجلالية القهرية

rows.speaker: البقلي
rows.claim: Al-Baqli says the veiling is left unexplained because intellect cannot grasp its reality; the pre-eternal God is beyond inhabiting places, and the tree was a mirror of divine manifestation.
rows.anchor: وقال البقلي رحمه الله : أبهم ما غشيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaygh means deviation from uprightness; the Prophet's sight did not turn even slightly away from what he saw.
rows.anchor: الزيغ الميل عن الاستقامة أي ما مال بصر رسول الله عليه السلام أدنى ميل عما رآه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He neither exceeded bounds amid overwhelming sights, but retained them accurately, nor turned from the marvels he was enabled and commanded to see.
rows.anchor: وما تجاوز مع ما شاهد هناك من الأمور المذهلة مما لا يحصى بل أثبته إثباتا صحيحا متيقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author's preferred inference is that the Prophet saw God with physical eyesight while awake: describing the eye as steady indicates waking vision, whereas a heart-vision would mention the heart.
rows.anchor: واستدل على أن رؤية الله كانت بعين بصره عليه السلام يقظة بقوله ما زاغ البصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative that baṣar means inner sight is possible in isolation, but the author rejects it because the passage supplies no contextual evidence for that reading.
rows.anchor: وأمال القول بأنه يجوز أن يكون المراد بالبصر بصر قلبه

rows.speaker: الكاشفي
rows.claim: Al-Kashifi says Muhammad's eye neither turned aside nor exceeded its permitted bounds; this praises his good etiquette and high aspiration, as he looked only toward the everlasting divine beauty.
rows.anchor: قال الكاشفي في معنى الآية : ميل نكرد شم محمد عليه السلام وي وراست ننكريست ودرنكذشت

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reads this as the Prophet's total poverty of self: his bodily sight ignored worldly attractions, his spiritual sight ignored afterlife rewards, and both attended wholly to God, His names, attributes, and manifestations.
rows.anchor: وفي التأويلات النجمية يشير إلى تحقق النبي عليه السلام بمقام حقيقة الفقر الكلي الذي هو الخلو المطلق عما سواه

rows.speaker: البقلي
rows.claim: Al-Baqli applies the verse to the second vision: the first had nothing besides God, while this one shows the beloved's complete steadiness and desire to behold his Lord without turning even toward a noble thing.
rows.anchor: وقال البقلي رحمه الله : هذه الآية في الرؤية الثانية لأن في الرؤية الأولى لم يكن شيء دون الله

rows.speaker: كشف الأسرار
rows.claim: Kashf al-Asrār contrasts Moses, who asked to see God and received 'You will not see Me' before repenting, with Muhammad, whose gaze was divinely guarded and praised as unwavering.
rows.anchor: وفي كشف الأسرار موسى عليه السلام ون ديدار خواست كه أرني أنظر إليك اورا بصمصام غيرت لن تراني جواب دادند

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anything that distances a person from God's presence is worldly life; seeking asceticism, piety, disclosures, or miracles for popularity, fame, status, or wealth wastes one's spiritual states and deeds without reward.
rows.anchor: فمن قصد بالزهد والورع والتقى والكشف والكرامات وخوارق العادات قبول الناس والشهرة عندهم وحصول الجاه والمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not be deceived by apparent unveiling or worldly acclaim: these may be immediate returns, as Iblis's nine thousand years of worship were followed by respite after his disbelief.
rows.anchor: ولا يغترن هذا بحصول بعض الكشوف وإقبال أهل الدنيا عليه فإنه ثمرة عاجلة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes dhālika to refer to their desire for worldly life.
rows.anchor: {ذالك} أي أمر اردنيا وفي بحرالعلوم

rows.speaker: بحر العلوم
rows.claim: Bahr al-ʿUlūm identifies the referent as choosing worldly life over the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وفي بحرالعلوم أي إرادة الدنيا وإيثارها على الآخرة

rows.speaker: الإرشاد
rows.claim: Al-Irshād identifies it as what led them to turn away and restrict their desires to worldly life.
rows.anchor: وفي الإرشاد أي ما أداهم إلى ما هم فيه من التولي وقصر الإرادة على الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mablagh means their limit of knowledge: they scarcely pass beyond worldly concerns to benefit from admonition, and al-ʿilm here includes false conjectural perception.
rows.anchor: لا يكادون يجاوزونه إلى غيره حتى يجديهم الدعوة والإرشاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mablagh is a place or extent noun; the pronoun is plural because min is construed by meaning here, whereas the earlier singular follows its grammatical form.
rows.anchor: فبلغ اسم مكان وجمع الضمير في مبلغهم باعتباره معنى من كما أن أفراده فيما سبق باعتبار لفظها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause interrupts the address to affirm how their ambition is confined to low worldly life; 30:7 similarly says they know the outward side of worldly life but are heedless of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والجملة اعتراض مقرر لقصر همتهم على الدنيا الدنية

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says God created nothing more hateful to Him than the world and has not looked toward it since creating it, out of hatred.
rows.anchor: إن الله لم يخلق خلقا هو أبغض إليه من الدنيا وما نظر إليها منذ خلقها بغضا لها رواه أبو هريرة رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world is not an end in itself but a path to what is truly intended; the Prophet likens it to a bridge to cross, not a place to build on.
rows.anchor: ومعنى هو أن الدنيا على الله سبحانه أنه تعالى لم يجعلها مقصودة لنفسه بل جعلها طريقا موصلة إلى ما هو المقصود لنفسه

rows.speaker: النبي عليه السلام
rows.claim: A prophetic saying calls the world a bridge: cross it rather than settling and building there.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال عليه السلام : الدنيا قنطرة فاعبروها لا تعمروها

rows.speaker: بعض أهل الحقيقة
rows.claim: Some people of spiritual realization say whatever distracts a person from the Master is that person's world and a source of ill fortune.
rows.anchor: كما قال بعض أهل الحقيقة : ما ألهاك عن مولاك فهو دنياك ومشؤوم عليك

rows.speaker: النبي عليه السلام
rows.claim: A prophetic saying forbids reviling the world, calling it the believer's excellent mount for reaching good and escaping evil; when cursed, it answers by cursing the most disobedient to God.
rows.anchor: كما قال عليه السلام : لا تسبوا الدنيا فنعمت مطية المؤمن عليها يبلغ الخير وبها ينجو من الشر
